_readme: The facts the two runtimes of this project have to agree on.
The Python gateway (repo root) and the SvelteKit front door (web/) are
separate programs in two languages, and they meet over HTTP, over a
PostgreSQL database, and over the identity of the player. Every value
that crosses one of those seams used to be written down twice, once per
language, with nothing checking that the two copies still matched.
That is not a style problem. When the front door bound port 3000 while
the origin compiled into the build said 8080, every page loaded and
every form was refused with 403 'Cross-site POST form submissions are
forbidden' -- the login included -- and nothing in either language said
the two disagreed.
This file is the single place those values are written down. The Python
side reads it through contract.py; the web side reads it through
web/src/lib/server/config.ts. Both test suites read it and assert that
what each runtime resolved matches what is written here, so a value
that drifts fails the build instead of the game.
Environment variables still win over everything in this file: this is
where the defaults live, not where a deployment is configured.

database._readme: The one PostgreSQL server for the whole project: the gateway's saves and the front door's accounts share it.
database.name: raisetheempires

gateway._readme: The AMF0 gateway. Loopback only: the front door is its only door.

public._readme: The front door. The port has to be the port of PUBLIC_ORIGIN, or every form POST is refused as cross-site.

_readme: How the front door hands the signed-in account's identity to the gateway.
Both are set by the front door and never forwarded from the client:
the proxy copies whatever the browser sent, so a player must not be
able to claim an identity by sending the header itself.
The role is the front door's to declare. It owns the accounts and the
roles; the gateway owns the saves. Asking the gateway to look the role
up in the accounts table would make it depend on another runtime's
schema, which is how the two halves drifted apart in the first place.
The gateway trusts the header for the same reason it trusts the id: it
listens on loopback and the front door is its only door.
The gateway routes that change game state or expose another player's data.
These used to be gated by a list of paths in the web front door, and
by nothing at all in the gateway: bind the gateway to 0.0.0.0 and
/list_session handed over every player's session id, DELETE /save
deleted any empire, and /patch/... granted any resource. The front
door's gate was the only lock, and it lives in another runtime.
The gateway now checks this list itself, so the lock is on the data
as well as on the door. The front door reads the same list and adds
its own routes to it.
A path in `exact` is admin-only on its own; a prefix in `prefixes`
is admin-only together with whatever follows it.
The environment variables the two runtimes read, by their canonical name.
The same deployment configures both halves, so a fact that crosses the
seam has to have ONE name. It used to have two: the gateway called the
database `SAVE_STORE_PATH` and the front door called it `RTE_DB_URL`, and
the front door called the origin `PUBLIC_ORIGIN` and the gateway called it
`WEB_ORIGIN`. An operator who set one of each pair left the two halves
pointing at different places: the gateway wrote saves to a database the
front door never read.
The old names still work -- they are listed as aliases -- but they are
not written down any more, and they lose to the canonical name when both
are set.
The shape of the payload the SWF asks the hosting page for.
The client has no social network of its own: during setup it calls
getUserInfo(), getFriendData() and getAppFriendIds() and reads fields
off what they return. If the user object comes back without `zid`, the
client does not degrade, it dies with Error #1009 before anything is
playable.
The gateway produces this and the front door consumes it, so the shape
is written down here once and both sides are checked against it.
The shape of /player.json, which the gateway produces and the account
page and the empire editor consume.
It replaced the front door's own `progress` table, which nothing in the
game ever wrote to: a player sat at level 1 next to a level 85 empire.
The resources the world keeps, in the order the 2012 editor showed them.
The gateway counts them in this order and the front door draws them in
it. Note that the order does not survive the wire: Flask sorts the keys
of a JSON object, so what the front door receives is alphabetical and
its own catalogue is what the player sees.
A new alliance starts like this, and this is the whole list of shields.
The web front door and the gateway both create alliances, from the
page and from inside the game, and they used to write the same
numbers twice. The gateway also accepted any shield, so an alliance
created in the game could carry one the page does not know about.

zid._readme: The player's stable id. CRC-64/GO-ISO divided down so the result is an exact integer for the Flash client, which has no integer type.
